title: A Genetic Variant Carried by 1 in 13 South Asians Makes the Standard Diabetes Blood Test Unreliable. Researchers Say Thousands of Cases Are Being Missed.
excerpt: Two separate studies have found that common genetic variants in South Asian and Black populations artificially lower HbA1c results — the test your doctor uses to diagnose and monitor diabetes. The implications for the Indian diaspora are enormous.
body:
If you are South Asian and your doctor tells you your blood sugar is fine based on an HbA1c test, you might want to ask a few more questions.

Two recent studies — one from researchers at the University of Exeter and Queen Mary University of London, the other a March 2026 preprint analysing more than 63,000 participants in the UK Biobank — have converged on a finding that should change how diabetes is screened in every diaspora clinic from Edison to Southall.

## The Problem With HbA1c

HbA1c, or glycated haemoglobin, is the gold standard for diagnosing and monitoring type 2 diabetes worldwide. It measures how much glucose has attached to your red blood cells over the previous two to three months. A reading of 6.5 per cent or higher means diabetes. Between 5.7 and 6.4 per cent means prediabetes.

The test works well — if your red blood cells behave the way the test assumes they do.

For millions of South Asians, they do not.

## PIEZO1: The Variant Hiding in Plain Sight

The March 2026 preprint identified a missense variant in the PIEZO1 gene carried by approximately one in 13 South Asians. The variant is extremely rare in other populations. Among more than 63,000 UK Biobank participants, carriers showed significantly lower HbA1c and altered red blood cell traits — but no difference in fasting glucose or C-peptide, the direct measures of blood sugar and insulin production.

In other words, their actual blood sugar was the same. The test just could not see it.

The researchers modelled the downstream consequences: approximately 1,019 missed prediabetes diagnoses and 303 missed type 2 diabetes diagnoses per 100,000 South Asian adults over ten years. Each missed prediabetes diagnosis is also a missed referral to a diabetes prevention programme. The estimated cost, in the UK's NHS system alone, runs between £970,000 and £1.39 million per 100,000 individuals over a decade.

## G6PD Deficiency: A Known Blind Spot, Largely Ignored

The Exeter study, published with support from a Wellcome Discovery Award, tackled a related but distinct problem. G6PD deficiency — a genetic condition that affects how red blood cells metabolise glucose — is carried by about one in 63 South Asian men and one in seven Black men in the UK. Fewer than one in 50 of those carriers has been diagnosed with the condition.

G6PD deficiency does not cause diabetes. But it makes HbA1c readings appear artificially low. The study found that men with G6PD deficiency were, on average, diagnosed with type 2 diabetes four years later than those without the variant.

Four years is a long time when diabetes is silently damaging kidneys, eyes, and blood vessels.

"Our findings highlight the urgent need for changes to testing practices to tackle health inequalities," said Professor Inês Barroso from the University of Exeter. "Doctors and health policy makers need to be aware that the HbA1c test may not be accurate for people with G6PD deficiency."

## What This Means for Indian Americans

South Asians are already four times more likely to develop type 2 diabetes than Europeans, often at a lower body weight and younger age. A May 2026 study in Scientific Reports surveying 215 South Asians in the United States found significant gaps in diabetes knowledge — the most frequently missed questions were about recognising the symptoms of low blood sugar.

Now add a diagnostic blind spot on top of that elevated risk. The standard screening test — the one your annual physical relies on — may be systematically understating your blood sugar if you carry either the PIEZO1 variant or G6PD deficiency. Neither condition is routinely screened for in the United States.

## What to Ask Your Doctor

If you are South Asian and relying solely on HbA1c for diabetes screening or monitoring, consider requesting supplementary tests:

**Fasting plasma glucose** — measures blood sugar directly, unaffected by red blood cell variants.

**Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)** — the two-hour test that tracks how your body handles a glucose load. It remains the most sensitive screening tool for prediabetes.

**Fructosamine** — measures average blood sugar over two to three weeks using a different mechanism than HbA1c.

If you have a family history of diabetes — and most South Asian families do — these additional tests are not excessive. They are corrective.

The science is now clear: the test that works for most of the world may not work for you. The responsible move is not to panic but to adapt. Talk to your doctor. Get the additional screening. And if you are already being managed for diabetes on the basis of HbA1c alone, ask whether your targets need to be recalibrated.

Your grandmother did not have access to this information. You do.

*Sources: PHG Foundation, University of Exeter Biomedical Research Centre, UK Biobank PIEZO1 preprint (March 2026), Scientific Reports (May 2026)*
